questions.text: Moving from linear scripts to engineered systems takes four structural pillars. Match each pillar to the topics it covers.
questions.explanation: Slide “Moving from linear scripts to engineered systems requires four structural pillars”: Foundation (modules & packages), Structural Integrity (exceptions & mutability), Architecture (object-oriented design) and Utilities (generators & file I/O).

questions.text: Match each pillar to the job it does.
questions.explanation: Slide “Moving from linear scripts to engineered systems requires four structural pillars”: each pillar's caption — organizing materials, preventing system collapse, creating scalable blueprints, interacting with the outside world.

questions.text: What do modules do, according to the slides?
options: Merge all of a program's code into one large file
Separate monolithic code into specialized, reusable toolboxes
Translate Python into machine code ahead of time
Stop a program from crashing when an error occurs
questions.explanation: Slide “Modules separate monolithic code into specialized, reusable toolboxes”.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Slide “Modules separate monolithic code…” (Broad Import): import math brings in the whole toolbox, and you reach a tool through the module name. math.sqrt() always returns a float, so it prints 5.0. Verified by running it.

questions.text: After import math, you can call sqrt(25) directly, without the math. prefix.
questions.explanation: A broad import only brings in the module name, so its tools must be reached as math.sqrt(25). Plain sqrt(25) raises NameError: name 'sqrt' is not defined (verified by running it). To call it bare you'd need from math import sqrt.

questions.text: After this import, how do you call the function?
questions.explanation: Slide “Modules separate monolithic code…” (Specific Import): from … import … as … takes just that one tool and gives it a new name, so you call random_num(1, 100). The name random itself is never imported, so random.randint raises NameError (verified by running it).

questions.text: Fill in the keyword that renames the imported function.
questions.code:
from random import randint ___ random_num
random_num(1, 100)
questions.explanation: Slide “Modules separate monolithic code…”: from random import randint as random_num — as gives the imported name an alias.

questions.text: Which file transforms a standard folder into a Python package?
questions.explanation: Slide “Packages scale local modules, while PIP connects you to the global ecosystem”: __init__.py “transforms standard folder into a Package”.

questions.text: Fill in the tool that downloads the requests package from PyPI.
questions.explanation: Slide “Packages scale local modules, while PIP connects you to the global ecosystem”: pip install requests pulls the package from PyPI over the PIP network, after which import requests works.

questions.text: What is PyPI?
options: The global Python Package Index that pip downloads packages from
A file that turns a folder into a package
Python's standard library module for networking
questions.explanation: Slide “Packages scale local modules, while PIP connects you to the global ecosystem”: PyPI is the Global Python Package Index; PIP connects your project to it.

questions.explanation: Slide “Unhandled runtime errors act as concrete roadblocks…”: without safeguards, one unexpected input acts as a fatal collision, bringing the entire system down instantly.

questions.text: Match each block of the exception-handling flow to when it runs.
allChoices: The main execution — the code that might fail
Only when a failure is caught (e.g. ValueError)
Only when the try block succeeded
Always, whether it succeeded or failed — execution complete

pairs.match: The main execution — the code that might fail
Only when a failure is caught (e.g. ValueError)
Only when the try block succeeded
Always, whether it succeeded or failed — execution complete

questions.explanation: Slide “Structural safeguards elegantly reroute failures to prevent system collapse”: main execution enters TRY. On success it takes the ELSE path, on a caught failure the EXCEPT path, and both paths meet at FINALLY.

questions.text: What does this print when raw = 'abc'?
questions.context:
try:
    n = int(raw)
except ValueError:
    print('Bad input')
else:
    print('Got', n)
finally:
    print('Done')
questions.explanation: Slide “Structural safeguards elegantly reroute failures…”: int('abc') raises ValueError, so the EXCEPT path runs and ELSE is skipped. FINALLY always runs. With raw = '42' it would print Got 42 then Done. Verified by running both.

questions.text: Match each level of the exception hierarchy to how it's described.
allChoices: Broadest scope — catches almost everything, but obscures the root cause

pairs.match: Broadest scope — catches almost everything, but obscures the root cause

questions.explanation: Slide “Exceptions are structurally hierarchical, requiring targeted precision”: ZeroDivisionError is a kind of ArithmeticError, which is a kind of Exception.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.context:
try:
    1 / 0
except ArithmeticError:
    print('A')
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print('Z')
questions.explanation: Slide “Exceptions are structurally hierarchical…”: ZeroDivisionError is a subclass of ArithmeticError, so the first handler matches. Python runs only the first matching except block, so the more specific one below it never gets a chance. That's why specific handlers go first. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Why do engineered systems avoid catching a generic Exception everywhere?
options: Because catching Exception is a syntax error
Because it catches almost everything but obscures the root cause — specific failures should be anticipated instead
Because generic handlers make the program run slower
questions.explanation: Slide “Exceptions are structurally hierarchical…”: Exception has the broadest scope and catches almost everything, but obscures the root cause. “Engineered systems anticipate specific failures rather than deploying generic catch-alls.”

questions.text: In the blueprint analogy, what is shirt?
options: An object (instance) built from the Item class
A module imported from the standard library
questions.explanation: Slide “Classes provide the blueprint; Objects represent the physical construction”: Item is the blueprint, and the T-Shirt, Hat and Shoes are the buildings made from it. shirt is one of those objects.

questions.text: Fill in the special method that runs automatically when Item('T-Shirt', 20.00) creates a new object.
questions.explanation: Slide “Classes provide the blueprint…”: the blueprint lists __init__(self, name, price), the constructor that sets up each new object's data.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.context:
class Item:
    def __init__(self, name, price):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price

    def apply_discount(self, percent):
        self.price = self.price * (1 - percent / 100)

shirt = Item('T-Shirt', 20.00)
shirt.apply_discount(10)
print(shirt.price)
questions.explanation: The slide only shows apply_discount(self, percent)'s signature; this body is a straightforward version of it. 10% off 20.00 is 20 × 0.9 = 18.0, and because it updates self.price, the object itself changes. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.context:
class Character:
    def __init__(self, hp):
        self.hp = hp

    def take_damage(self, amount):
        self.hp -= amount

class Knight(Character):
    def take_damage(self, amount):
        self.hp -= max(0, amount - 5)

k = Knight(100)
k.take_damage(3)
k.take_damage(20)
print(k.hp)
questions.explanation: Slide “Inheritance scales architecture by eliminating redundant blueprints”: Knight inherits hp from Character but overrides take_damage with max(0, amount - 5). A 3-damage hit becomes max(0, -2) = 0; a 20-damage hit becomes 15. 100 − 0 − 15 = 85. A plain Character would end at 77. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Fill in the parent class so that Knight inherits from Character.
questions.explanation: Slide “Inheritance scales architecture…”: the parent class goes in the parentheses after the class name, so Knight inherits everything Character has.

questions.text: Custom exceptions use the same inheritance model. Fill in the base class.
questions.explanation: Slide “Inheritance scales architecture…”, Note: custom exceptions like NegativeNumberError branch off Python's base Exception class. Verified that it can then be raised and caught like any built-in exception.

questions.text: What does the with statement guarantee here?
options: The file is opened for writing and erased first
The file is closed automatically when the block ends, even if the code inside crashes
The file is copied into memory and the original is deleted
The program never raises an error while the file is open
questions.explanation: Slide “Context managers operate as secure airlocks for external system interactions”: 1. open access, 2. secure processing, 3. auto-seal (close). It automatically and safely closes the file to prevent resource leaks, regardless of internal crashes.

questions.text: Inside a with open(...) as file: block, you still have to call file.close() yourself to avoid resource leaks.
questions.explanation: Slide “Context managers operate as secure airlocks…”: the auto-seal step closes the file for you when the block ends, even after a crash. No manual close() needed.

questions.text: What does this print?
questions.context:
def count_up(n):
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        yield i
        i += 1

g = count_up(3)
print(next(g), next(g))
questions.explanation: Slide “Generators utilize lazy evaluation to process infinite data at scale”: yield makes this a generator, which processes one item at a time, on demand. Each next() resumes it just long enough to produce the next value: 0, then 1. Verified by running it.

questions.text: You need to process 1,000,000 records. Why would a generator beat a normal function that builds and returns a list?
options: A generator stores all 1,000,000 items at once, so lookups are faster
A generator uses lazy evaluation, producing one item at a time instead of holding every item in memory
A generator automatically runs on multiple CPU cores
A generator converts the records into a tuple so they can't be changed
questions.explanation: Slide “Generators utilize lazy evaluation…”: a normal function returning a list is eager — memory overload from storing 1,000,000 items simultaneously. A generator (yield) is lazy and processes one item at a time, on demand.

questions.text: What does os.getcwd() return?
options: The path of the current working directory, as a string
A list of every file on the computer
The name of the operating system
questions.explanation: Slide “The Standard Library provides pre-engineered utilities…”: os navigates the filesystem, and getcwd() means “get current working directory”. It returns that path as a string (verified by running it).

questions.text: The slide writes datetime.now(). Which import makes that line work exactly as written?
questions.warning: datetime.now() on its own hides which import it needs. After a plain import datetime it fails — you'd need datetime.datetime.now().
questions.explanation: The datetime module contains a datetime class, and now() belongs to the class. from datetime import datetime brings in the class, so datetime.now() works. After a plain import datetime, datetime.now() raises AttributeError: module 'datetime' has no attribute 'now'. Verified by running both.

questions.text: Match each stage of “The Anatomy of a Python Application” to the code that represents it.
questions.explanation: Slide “The Anatomy of a Python Application”: a package brings data in, an OOP class processes it inside a try/except shield, and generators plus file I/O send it out. “Scripts execute lines. Systems orchestrate data.”
